title: Calling a function on another machine
objective: By the end of this lesson you can describe what a remote call adds to a local one, name the failure that has no local equivalent, and design an interface that survives being called over a network.

blocks.text: A remote procedure call is meant to look like an ordinary function call: you call something, it runs elsewhere, you get a result. The appeal is obvious and the trap is exactly the same thing — code that looks local but is not, written by people who then reason about it as if it were.

items: Your arguments are serialised into bytes
Those bytes travel over the connection this course has been building
The far side deserialises them and calls the real function
Its return value is serialised and sent back
Your side deserialises it and returns, as if nothing had happened

blocks.text: Every step can fail, and steps two and four can fail in a way that leaves you unable to tell what happened. That is the whole difficulty, and everything below follows from it.

rows: The process crashes, and you know
The call may or may not have run
Copied and encoded; large ones are expensive
The other end may be restarting, or gone
Two sides may be running different versions right now

blocks.title: The failure with no local equivalent
blocks.text: A timeout does not tell you whether the far side ran your call. The request may have been lost on the way, or it may have executed and the reply lost on the way back. Locally there is no equivalent of this — the function either ran or it did not. Every design decision below exists because of this one property, and any system that retries without accounting for it will eventually perform an operation twice.

The HTTP lesson introduced the idea that some operations may be repeated with the same end result. That is the property a remote interface needs, and when the operation does not have it naturally, it can be given it.

blocks.caption: An operation that cannot be repeated, and the same one made safe
lines: /* Unsafe: retrying after a timeout may charge twice. */
/* Safe: the caller generates a unique key; the server remembers it. */
if this request_id was already processed:
return the recorded result, do not charge again
charge, record the result against the id, return it
The retry now produces the same answer as the original, which is
what makes it safe for a client to retry without knowing whether

blocks.text: Designing an interface for a network

items: Coarse rather than fine: one call that fetches an order with its lines beats ten calls, because latency is paid per call
Explicit failure in the signature: a caller must be able to distinguish 'no result' from 'failed'
Deadlines, not just timeouts: pass the remaining budget along so a chain of calls does not multiply
Version tolerantly: a receiver should ignore fields it does not know, and a sender should not require fields the other side may not send
Bound every payload: an unbounded list becomes an unbounded response and a memory problem

blocks.title: The mistake that produces most slow systems
blocks.text: Fine-grained interfaces feel clean — one call per thing — and they are how you would design locally, where a call costs nothing. Over a network, a loop that makes one call per item pays the round trip per item. A hundred items over a 5 ms link is half a second of pure waiting. This is the single most common performance problem in distributed systems, and it is a design decision rather than an optimisation problem.

rows: Work that need not be answered immediately
Rare, and usually a mistake unless you measured a reason

blocks.text: All of these run on top of what this module built. A remote call is a request and a response over a connection, with a serialisation format and a set of conventions layered on — and knowing that is what lets you debug one with tcpdump rather than only with the framework's own tooling.

blocks.title: Turn your server into an RPC service
steps: Extend the capstone protocol so the message body starts with an operation name and its arguments
Implement two operations: one that is safe to repeat, and one that is not — for example a counter increment
Call the unsafe one, kill the reply before it arrives, and have the client retry — observe the double effect
Add a request identifier and have the server remember results by it
Retry again and confirm the result is now the same as the original
Write a client that fetches 100 items with 100 calls, and time it
Add one call that fetches all 100 and compare the times
Introduce an artificial 5 ms delay per call and repeat both measurements
blocks.expected: A double effect you caused on purpose and then eliminated with a request identifier, and a batched call that is dramatically faster than the loop. The 5 ms delay makes the second point unmissable: interface granularity, not code efficiency, is what determined the result.

cheatsheet: A remote call serialises arguments, sends them, executes remotely, and returns a serialised result
Latency is six orders of magnitude higher than a local call
A timeout does not tell you whether the call ran — this has no local equivalent
Make operations repeatable, or give each request a unique id the server remembers
Design coarse interfaces: latency is paid per call, not per byte
One call per item over a 5 ms link costs 5 ms per item
Pass deadlines along a chain so timeouts do not multiply
Version tolerantly: ignore unknown fields, do not require new ones
Bound every payload, or an unbounded list becomes an unbounded response

checkpoint.prompt: A remote call times out. What do you know about whether it executed?

choices.C: Nothing — the request may have been lost, or it may have run and the reply lost

checkpoint.explanation: This ambiguity has no local equivalent and is the reason remote interfaces need repeatable operations or request identifiers. Retrying without one eventually performs an operation twice.

checkpoint.prompt: A client fetches 100 items with 100 calls over a link with 5 ms round-trip time. Roughly how long does it take?

choices.B: About 500 ms — the round trip is paid once per call
choices.D: Depends only on the payload size

checkpoint.explanation: Latency is per call. This is why coarse interfaces matter, and why the fix is a design change rather than a faster implementation.

checkpoint.prompt: How do you make a charge operation safe to retry?

choices.A: Make the client check the balance first
choices.D: Have the caller supply a unique request id that the server records, returning the original result on a repeat

checkpoint.explanation: The server can then tell an original from a repeat. Checking the balance first is a check-then-act race, which is the same defect as the operating systems course's TOCTOU bug.

checkpoint.prompt: Why pass a deadline rather than only a timeout through a chain of calls?

choices.C: Each hop with its own timeout adds up
choices.D: Timeouts are not supported over HTTP

checkpoint.explanation: A chain can wait far longer than the caller intended. Three hops with a 5 second timeout each can take 15 seconds. Passing the remaining budget lets each hop know how much time is actually left.
